summary: Fireguard turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots for Chile and Argentina into one consistent record, and shows where fire activity is most likely tomorrow. VIIRS sees about three times as many hotspots as MODIS for the same fires, so raw counts jump in 2012 because of the sensor, not the fire; with MODIS ending in 2027, today's detections would lose their history. We put 7 million quality-checked MODIS and VIIRS detections (2000-2026) on one VIIRS-equivalent scale, with factors per region, month and satellite pass. On years the factors never saw, the yearly total is off by about 2% in Argentina and 5% in Chile. A burn calendar compares every month and region with its usual level. On top, a next-day outlook tested on 2023-2025 catches 78-79% of the cells with fire activity and says why each one is flagged. One web map puts it in front of brigades and emergency teams: where to look first, and why.
details:
Fireguard puts 26 years (2000-2026) of NASA fire detections for Chile and Argentina on one scale, and shows where fire activity is most likely tomorrow.

MODIS and VIIRS do not count the same way: VIIRS sees about three hotspots for each one MODIS sees, so a 2005 map and a 2025 map cannot be compared directly. We cleaned 8 million FIRMS hotspots down to 7 million (no doubtful detections, industrial sites or volcanoes). Then we measured the gap between the two sensors in the years they overlap (2012 to 2021), by region, month and time of day, and converted everything to one unit: VIIRS-equivalent hotspots. When we hide a year and estimate it again, the error is about 2% in Argentina and 5% in Chile.

With that series we built a burn calendar for any region and period, on 0.25° cells, that compares each month with its median of the other years, so an unusual season stands out.

On that series, one LightGBM model per country gives each 25 km cell a chance of fire for the next day, and states the reason for every alert in plain words. Tested on 2023 to 2025, years the model never saw, it catches about 8 of 10 cells that have fire the next day. With the same number of alerts, a simple "fire today nearby" rule catches 64% in Argentina and 49% in Chile. Fireguard catches 79% and 68%.

For each fire seen today, the map shows the chance it is detected again and the zone where its next hotspots usually fall: on 2023-2025, 83% of next-day hotspots fell inside the 80% zone.

The web map has three views: History (is this normal?), Now (the last 14 days, with wind) and Outlook (where to look tomorrow), with NASA GIBS satellite imagery of the same day under the hotspots. It is made for brigades and emergency teams that must decide where to look first.

Two choices are our own. We count by fire day, from 06:00 to 06:00 local solar time, so one night of burning is not split in two. And every alert comes with its reason, not only a score.

What we were careful about: a hotspot is a satellite detection, not a fire and not burned area. Values before 2012 are estimates. The outlook does not say where a fire will start, and most alerts end with no fire. Weather is not in the model yet.

Built with Python, DuckDB, LightGBM, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, deck.gl and MapLibre, with 149 automated tests. Data: NASA FIRMS and NASA GIBS imagery, and Open-Meteo for wind. The code is open, and the method works in any country FIRMS covers.

Use of AI: we used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant for coding, debugging and editing the English text. The method, the data choices and every number were checked by the team against the data. Commits made with it carry a "Co-Authored-By" line in the repository.
dataRefs: FIRMS active fire data: MODIS C6.1 (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21)
NASA GIBS imagery (VIIRS NOAA-20 / MODIS Terra corrected reflectance)
